blog/binary-search-on-the-answer/index.h.description: Binary search can narrow a capacity estimate when the pass criterion is stable and monotone. The difficult part is making a load test satisfy those conditions.
blog/binary-search-on-the-answer/index.h.title: Binary search on the answer · Tomas Brasca
blog/binary-search-on-the-answer/index.h.prose: There is a family of contest problems where the trick is to stop searching the input and start searching the answer. The canonical example: ship n packages within D days, minimizing truck capacity. Computing the optimal capacity directly is awkward. But checking a given capacity is trivial: greedily fill days, count them. And the check is monotone : if capacity c works, every capacity above c works too. Monotone predicate plus cheap check means binary search, not on the array, but on the answer itself: bool feasible ( long long cap ) { long long days = 1 , load = 0 ; for ( int w : weights) { if (w > cap) return false ; if (load + w > cap) { days ++ ; load = w; } else load += w; } return days <= D; } long long lo = 1 , hi = totalWeight; while (lo < hi) { long long mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2 ; if ( feasible (mid)) hi = mid; else lo = mid + 1 ; } // lo is the minimum feasible capacity The invariant carried through the loop: hi is always feasible-or-untested-upper-bound, lo - 1 is always infeasible. The answer is pinched between them, and each probe halves the gap. In contests this technique is so common it has a name (“binary search on the answer”) and the reflex it trains is the useful part: when the direct question is hard, ask whether the yes/no version is monotone. The production version is capacity planning “What is the maximum sustained RPS this service can handle?” is the same shape of question as the truck problem, and teams routinely answer it the awkward way: run one big load test at a guessed number, watch it fall over or not, guess again, argue about the guess. Reframe it as a predicate: feasible(rps) = at a sustained rps for two minutes, p99 latency stays under 400 ms and the error rate stays under 0.1%. Treat monotonicity as an assumption to establish under controlled conditions, not as a property guaranteed by a service. With fixed resources and comparable state, a lower request rate should be no harder than a higher one. (Where monotonicity genuinely breaks, caches that only warm up under load, autoscalers with hysteresis, you have learned something more important than the number. More on that below.) Monotone predicate, expensive-but-automatable check, bounded answer space. Binary search: async function findCeiling ( lo : number , hi : number ) : Promise < number > { // invariant: lo is known-feasible, hi is known-infeasible while (hi - lo > 25 ) { const mid = Math. floor ((lo + hi) / 2 ); ( await holdsAt (mid)) ? (lo = mid) : (hi = mid); } return lo; // observed feasible; bracket width is at most 25 RPS } Each probe is a two-minute load test. Searching an established 0–3,200 RPS bracket to a 25-RPS resolution takes seven midpoint probes. At two minutes per probe, that is fourteen minutes of measurement, before warm-up, cool-down, bracketing, and confirmation runs. The one-big-test approach burns the same fifteen minutes producing a single yes/no at a number someone guessed. Two details carry over from the contest version, and both are the kind of thing the judge punishes you for forgetting: Bracket before you search. The contest loop needs lo infeasible-adjacent and hi feasible (or vice versa) before the first iteration. The production equivalent: confirm the service survives the floor and fails at the ceiling before bisecting. If it holds at your chosen hi , you have no bracket, and a search inside a broken bracket converges confidently to nonsense. The check must be hermetic. In contests, feasible() must not mutate state between probes, or the search lies to you. In load testing the equivalent sins are connection pools still draining from the previous probe, autoscaling triggered by probe four contaminating probe five, and caches warmed by earlier rounds. Cool-down between probes is not politeness; it is the precondition for the invariant. When the predicate is not monotone The truck problem is monotone by construction. Production sometimes is not: I have watched a service pass at 900 RPS and fail at 600, because at 900 the autoscaler had already kicked in and at 600 it idled below the scale-up threshold while a single instance saturated. A binary search will not tell you this; it assumes monotonicity rather than checking it. The cheap defense: after the search converges, re-probe the claimed ceiling and one point well below it. If the “easier” point repeatedly fails under comparable conditions, the monotonicity assumption is unsupported, and the real finding is the non-monotonicity itself: that autoscaler threshold was the actual bug, and no amount of searching would have surfaced it as crisply as one failed re-probe. Passing two confirmation probes is still not a proof of monotonicity. Repeat runs near the boundary, record uncertainty, and treat the result as a tested operating range rather than an exact physical ceiling. That, too, is a contest reflex. The technique is never the trick. Stating the conditions under which the technique is legal: that is the trick.

blog/building-editorial-ui/index.html.description: The constraints behind a small component library, and the packaging work needed to make its CSS and React components usable.
blog/building-editorial-ui/index.html.title: Building editorial-ui: hairlines over shadows · Tomas Brasca
blog/building-editorial-ui/index.html.prose: The first three hours of every side project were always the same: button radius, grey scale, which font, how much shadow. Then the next project, the same three hours, slightly different answers. Those answers rarely made a significant difference. They were just decisions, and decisions are expensive even when they don’t matter. The fix is not better taste. The fix is to make the decisions once, encode them, and never have the conversation again. So I built editorial-ui : a React component library on npm, designed for an audience of exactly one. A design system for one person A company design system mediates disagreement between people. A personal one eliminates choice for your future self. That second job is easier and, for a solo builder, more valuable; the enemy is not inconsistency across a team, it is re-litigating the same bikeshed every weekend. The trick is that a system this small does not need a token taxonomy or a governance doc. It needs a handful of constraints strict enough that most questions answer themselves. I ended up with four. Four constraints are the whole system One amber action per view. A single primary call-to-action is visually distinct; everything else is ghost, quiet, or danger. Hairlines over shadows. Dividers are 1px solid var(--rule) . Cards sit on the surface plane instead of floating above it. Warm paper surfaces. Backgrounds are warm off-white, never pure white or cool grey. Serif for reading, sans for UI. Newsreader appears at headings and quote titles; Geist handles interface text; JetBrains Mono is reserved for small-caps labels and never touches body copy. The constraints live in the token file, not in a style guide nobody reads. This is the top of tokens.css , verbatim: :root { /* Paper surfaces */ --paper : #fbfaf6 ; --paper-2 : #f4f2ec ; --paper-3 : #ece9df ; /* Ink */ --ink : #1a1814 ; --ink-2 : #3a362f ; --muted : #807a6f ; --muted-2 : #b5aea0 ; /* Hairlines */ --rule : #e5e0d5 ; --rule-2 : #d9d3c5 ; /* Amber (one per surface) */ --amber : #f2a03c ; --amber-deep : #c77a1f ; --amber-soft : #fbe6c8 ; } Note the comment on the amber block. The rule is written where the colour is defined, so you cannot reach for --amber without reading it. There is no generic --gray-50 through --gray-900 ramp because a ramp is a menu, and menus invite choosing. Three papers, two inks, two rules. If a screen needs more than that, it might be getting too complex. The fifth rule, implicit in the other four: no new colours . Every colour reference goes through a variable. Dark mode then becomes a token swap ( :root[data-theme="dark"] redefines the same names) instead of a second stylesheet. The technical shape React components plus plain CSS files. No Tailwind, no CSS-in-JS, no PostCSS. The build is tsup with the CSS passed through untouched: // tsup.config.ts loader : { '.css' : 'copy' , }, tsup’s copy loader does not inline @import lines, so a small post-build script flattens styles/index.css into one self-contained bundle. That bundle matters because the package has a CSS-only entry : link editorial-ui/styles.css in a plain HTML page and write class="btn-amber" , no React required. The React components are a thin typed layer over those exact class names: Button with variant="amber" renders class="btn btn-amber" and nothing else. From the component source: const classNames = [ 'btn' , variant && `btn-${ variant }` , size !== 'md' && `btn-${ size }` , block && 'btn-block' , disabled && 'is-disabled' , className, ] . filter (Boolean) . join ( ' ' ); Why not Tailwind: Tailwind is a tool for making choices quickly, and the entire point of this library is that the choices are already made. Utility classes would hand back every decision I just removed. Why not CSS-in-JS: it adds a runtime, complicates server rendering, and makes the CSS-only entry impossible. Plain CSS files are inspectable in devtools exactly as written, diff cleanly against the design reference, and will still build in ten years. What “one amber action” did to the API The constraint that defines the system is the one the library cannot enforce . A React component cannot see its siblings across the tree; Button has no way to know another amber button exists on the same screen. So the API encodes the constraint as friction instead. variant is optional, and the default is the neutral style: < Button variant = "ghost" onClick = {onCancel}>Cancel</ Button > < Button variant = "amber" >Save</ Button > You opt in to prominence, never out of it. There is no primary prop that half the team sets out of habit; the word in the code is the colour on the screen, which makes a second amber button easy to spot in review. Every compound component ships the hierarchy pre-built: Modal.Footer examples pair a ghost cancel with one amber confirm, and the docs never show two ambers together, so copy-paste propagates the rule. The honest summary: the type system enforces which variants exist, the docs enforce how many , and review enforces the rest. A constraint that lives in convention is weaker than one that lives in the compiler, but it is much stronger than one that lives in nobody’s head. Publishing: the boring parts took longest The components were a focused sprint. Making the package consumable took longer than writing it, which I have come to accept as the normal shape of shipping . The two lines that absorbed the most debugging are in package.json : "sideEffects" : [ "**/*.css" ], "exports" : { "." : { "types" : "./dist/react/index.d.ts" , "import" : "./dist/react/index.js" }, "./react" : { "types" : "./dist/react/index.d.ts" , "import" : "./dist/react/index.js" }, "./fonts.css" : "./dist/styles/fonts.css" , "./tokens.css" : "./dist/styles/tokens.css" , "./styles.css" : "./dist/styles/index.css" , "./icons" : { "types" : "./dist/react/icons/index.d.ts" , "import" : "./dist/react/icons/index.js" } } The React entry auto-imports its stylesheet so consumers get styles for free. Without sideEffects declaring the CSS, bundlers tree-shake that import away and you ship unstyled buttons, silently, only in production builds. The exports map went through several rounds too: separate fonts.css and tokens.css entries exist so a Next.js app can self-host fonts and skip the Google Fonts import, and a post-build script prepends "use client" banners so the components survive the App Router. None of this is design. All of it decides whether anyone can actually use the thing. Eating it The quiet default view of this site started from these tokens: the hairlines between sections are var(--rule) , the background is var(--paper) , and those rules established the original visual baseline. The site has since added cinematic interpretations, while the portfolio agent replaced the router demo. This post records the library decisions; it is not a specification for every current page. Constraints beat choices. Four of them turned out to be a whole design system.

blog/data-structures-typescript-python/i.description: A practical map of arrays, queues, heaps, maps, and union-find, with the library differences and complexity traps to watch for in TypeScript and Python.
blog/data-structures-typescript-python/i.title: Data structures in TypeScript and Python · Tomas Brasca
blog/data-structures-typescript-python/i.prose: A data structure is a bet about which operation has to be fast. An array bets on random access. A hash map bets on key lookup. A heap bets that the only element you ever care about is the extreme one. Pick the structure whose bet matches the question your code keeps asking, and the complexity analysis mostly does itself. What changes between languages is not the bets; it is which ones the standard library has already placed for you. TypeScript and Python make different choices here, and the differences are exactly where interview code and production code go quietly quadratic. This post is the map I wish I’d had as one page: each structure, the question it answers in O(something good), and the one pattern per structure that does most of the work in practice. The map Structure Core bet Where you’ve already met it Array O(1) access by index Everywhere Stack O(1) at one end (LIFO) Undo/redo, the call stack Queue O(1) at both ends (FIFO) BFS, task scheduling Linked list O(1) insert/delete at a known node LRU cache internals Hash table O(1) average key lookup Every cache, every index Heap O(1) peek at min/max OS schedulers, Dijkstra Graph model relationships, traverse in O(V+E) Shortest-path anything Union-Find ”are these connected?” in ~O(1) Clustering, Kruskal’s MST Balanced BST sorted map, O(log n) everything Java’s TreeMap, C++ std::map B-tree family sorted keys with high fan-out Many database indexes Trie O(L) prefix lookup Every autocomplete box Suffix array O(m log n) substring search Bioinformatics, plagiarism detection Segment tree O(log n) range query with updates Time-series rollups Bloom filter membership test using a fixed set of hashes Avoiding unnecessary storage reads The last four rows you will rarely implement outside a contest. The value of having them in the table is recognition: when someone asks “what was the average CPU between 2pm and 4pm?”, you should hear range query over an array and know the answer space before opening an editor. One row gets no section below: graphs. Not because they matter less, but because traversal is a toolkit of its own, and BFS, DFS, and Dijkstra deserve more than a paragraph. That’s the follow-up post . What the languages actually hand you Here is the asymmetry that shapes everything below. Python gives you list , dict , set , heapq , and collections.deque . TypeScript gives you Array , Map , and Set , and that’s it. TypeScript has no heap, no deque, no sorted map; neither language has a linked list, trie, union-find, or segment tree. Their general-purpose lists and arrays are dynamic. JavaScript typed arrays and Python’s array module also provide typed numeric storage, while memoryview exposes a buffer without copying it. Capacity, copying, and element representation still matter for large workloads. Two practical consequences: The queue trap. A queue needs O(1) at both ends. Python’s list.pop(0) and TypeScript’s Array.shift() are both O(n): every remaining element shifts left. Python has the fix built in: from collections import deque queue = deque([start]) node = queue.popleft() # O(1) TypeScript does not. For interview-sized inputs, shift() is fine and everyone knows it; for production, you either keep a read-index into a plain array or bring a dependency. The point is to know you are making that trade, not to discover it in a profiler. The heap gap. Python’s heapq supplies min-heaps. Python 3.14 also adds public max-heap functions such as heappush_max and heappop_max . Negating numeric priorities remains a useful compatibility technique for older versions. See the Python heapq documentation . TypeScript has nothing, and this is the single most common “wait, really?” for people arriving from Python or Java. In an interview you say so out loud and write the simplest thing that preserves the interface: class SortedPriorityQueue { private heap : number [] = []; push ( val : number ) : void { this .heap. push (val); this .heap. sort (( a , b ) => a - b); // O(n log n) per push, say it then move on } pop () : number | undefined { return this .heap. shift (); } peek () : number | undefined { return this .heap[ 0 ]; } } That is not a heap. It is a sorted array wearing a heap’s interface. Naming the gap and bounding the cost is worth more than reproducing sift-up from memory under a clock. Arrays, and the one pattern that pays rent For everything beyond the basics, the leverage is not in the structure; it is in one pattern per structure that converts an O(n²) instinct into an O(n) solution. For arrays, that pattern is the prefix sum : spend O(n) once to build an accumulator, then answer any range-sum question in O(1). def build_prefix (nums: list[ int ]) -> list[ int ]: prefix = [ 0 ] * ( len (nums) + 1 ) for i, n in enumerate (nums): prefix[i + 1 ] = prefix[i] + n return prefix def range_sum (prefix: list[ int ], l: int , r: int ) -> int : return prefix[r + 1 ] - prefix[l] # sum of [l, r] inclusive, O(1) function buildPrefix ( nums : number []) : number [] { const prefix = new Array (nums. length + 1 ). fill ( 0 ); for ( let i = 0 ; i < nums. length ; i ++ ) prefix[i + 1 ] = prefix[i] + nums[i]; return prefix; } function rangeSum ( prefix : number [], l : number , r : number ) : number { return prefix[r + 1 ] - prefix[l]; } The off-by-one is load-bearing: the extra leading zero is what lets range_sum(prefix, 0, r) work without a special case. Prefix sums are the static answer to range queries; the moment the underlying array needs updates between queries, you have walked into segment-tree territory: same question, harder bet. Stacks: the monotonic trick A stack is a dynamic array you only touch at one end, and both languages do it natively with push / pop (or append / pop ), no ceremony. The pattern worth drilling is the monotonic stack : for each element, find the next greater (or smaller) element to its right, in O(n) instead of the naive O(n²). function nextGreater ( nums : number []) : number [] { const result = new Array (nums. length ). fill ( - 1 ); const stack : number [] = []; // indices of elements still waiting for their answer for ( let i = 0 ; i < nums. length ; i ++ ) { while (stack. length && nums[i] > nums[stack[stack. length - 1 ]]) { result[stack. pop () ! ] = nums[i]; } stack. push (i); } return result; } // [2,1,2,4,3] → [4,2,4,-1,-1] The invariant (the stack always holds indices of a non-increasing run) is what makes the amortized analysis one sentence: every index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the nested-looking loop is O(n). Stock-span, daily-temperatures, largest-rectangle-in-histogram are all this one trick in costume. Hash maps: store the complement, not the search Hash maps are useful when the dominant operation is lookup by key. Python dictionaries typically provide average O(1) access. JavaScript Map guarantees average sublinear access, not a particular hash-table implementation or an O(1) bound, and most “make it faster” interview answers are some form of “put a hash map in front of it.” The canonical pattern is two-sum: instead of scanning for a partner for each element (O(n²)), record what you’ve seen and ask whether the current element completes a pair: def two_sum (nums: list[ int ], target: int ) -> list[ int ]: seen: dict[ int , int ] = {} # value -> index for i, n in enumerate (nums): if target - n in seen: return [seen[target - n], i] seen[n] = i return [] The generalizable move is the reframe: don’t search forward for what you need; remember backward what you’ve had. Frequency counts, anagram grouping, and memoization are the same move with different keys. The ones you always build from scratch Linked lists, tries, and union-find exist in neither standard library, and that turns out to be fine: each is under twenty lines, and the lines are the same every time. Union-find is the one I’d actually memorize, because it answers a question nothing else answers cheaply: are these two things in the same group? , in O(α(n)) per query. α is the inverse Ackermann function, and α(n) ≤ 4 for any n that fits in hardware, so treat it as constant. class UnionFind : def __init__ (self, n: int ): self .parent = list ( range (n)) self .rank = [ 0 ] * n def find (self, x: int ) -> int : if self .parent[x] != x: self .parent[x] = self .find( self .parent[x]) # path compression return self .parent[x] def union (self, x: int , y: int ) -> bool : px, py = self .find(x), self .find(y) if px == py: return False if self .rank[px] < self .rank[py]: px, py = py, px self .parent[py] = px # union by rank if self .rank[px] == self .rank[py]: self .rank[px] += 1 return True Using both optimizations gives the usual inverse-Ackermann amortized bound: path compression flattens the tree as you query it, union by rank keeps it from growing tall in the first place. Connected components, cycle detection in undirected graphs, Kruskal’s MST, “do these accounts belong to the same person”: all union-find, all the same twenty lines. Linked lists earn their twenty lines differently: not as a container you’d reach for (O(n) to find anything), but as the only structure with O(1) delete at a known node, which is why the textbook LRU cache is a hash map pointing into a doubly linked list, and why the fast-and-slow-pointer trick (cycle detection, find-the-middle in one pass) keeps showing up. The LRU cache is worth thirty extra seconds, because it is the one interview classic that composes two structures: the hash map answers “do we have this key?” in O(1), the linked list answers “which entry is oldest?” in O(1), and every node is reachable from both. And here is where knowing your standard library’s bets pays off twice: JavaScript’s Map preserves insertion order. Its internal representation is engine-specific; that order guarantee is enough for the cache below. A full LRU in TypeScript is a dozen lines and no node class: class LRUCache < K , V > { private map = new Map < K , V >(); constructor ( private capacity : number ) { if ( ! Number. isInteger (capacity) || capacity < 0 ) { throw new RangeError ( 'capacity must be a nonnegative integer' ); } } get ( key : K ) : V | undefined { if ( ! this .map. has (key)) return undefined ; const val = this .map. get (key) ! ; this .map. delete (key); this .map. set (key, val); // re-insert → now the newest entry return val; } put ( key : K , val : V ) : void { if ( this .map. has (key)) this .map. delete (key); this .map. set (key, val); if ( this .map.size > this .capacity) { this .map. delete ( this .map. keys (). next ().value ! ); // first key = oldest } } } Python plays the same trick with collections.OrderedDict ( move_to_end on access, popitem(last=False) to evict), and if the cache fronts a pure function, functools.lru_cache is one decorator. The hand-rolled doubly-linked-list version is still worth understanding, because it explains the operations the cache needs, regardless of how a runtime implements them. But reaching for it first is solving a problem your standard library already solved. The ones you only reason about B-Trees and Bloom filters close the table, and the honest advice is: understand them, never implement them. A B+ Tree node is sized to one disk page, so hundreds of keys per node means a million-row index is three or four levels deep: three or four disk reads for any lookup. That explains one reason an appropriate B-tree index can reduce lookup work, and it is worth more in a system-design conversation than any implementation would be. A Bloom filter is the inverse trade: a few kilobits buy you “this key definitely doesn’t exist”, which is how RocksDB and Cassandra skip disk reads for absent keys: false positives possible, false negatives never. The pattern across this whole post is the same one: the structure is rarely the hard part. The hard part is hearing the question your code keeps asking ( next greater? same group? range with updates? definitely absent? ) and recognizing which bet, already placed and paid for, answers it. That recognition reflex is the part of contest training that actually transfers, which is its own post . For the JavaScript guarantees behind the cache, see the Map reference .

blog/evals-are-contracts/index.html.description: A routing decision needs a quality bar. Versioned datasets, explicit pass criteria, and a consequence for failing make that bar reviewable.
blog/evals-are-contracts/index.html.title: Evals are contracts · Tomas Brasca
blog/evals-are-contracts/index.html.prose: A router can send structured-output requests to a smaller model and improve every operational dashboard while making the product worse. If the eval dataset never covers nested objects, a green run says nothing about whether the model handles them. Support tickets may reveal the gap first. That failure might not be about routing. Routing is often the easy half: classify the request, dispatch to the cheapest model that clears the bar . The hard half is one word. Clears . Clears what? Measured how? Decided by whom? The load-bearing word The following sketches describe a simplified router. They are illustrative, not the current portfolio agent. Each catalog entry declares which request classes a model is allowed to serve: /** A cheap model we're willing to dispatch to, and the classes it clears. */ interface CatalogEntry { provider : string ; model : string ; keyName : string ; /** USD per 1M tokens, used to compute real cost and to rank by price. */ inPrice : number ; outPrice : number ; /** prompt classes this model is allowed to serve. */ clears : PromptClass []; } And dispatch is a walk down a cost-ordered list: function pickModel ( cls : PromptClass , env : Record < string , string | undefined >) : CatalogEntry | null { for ( const entry of CATALOG ) { if (entry.clears. includes (cls) && env[entry.keyName]) return entry; } return null ; } That clears array is the entire routing decision. Eight lines of dispatch, one array of truth. So the real question is upstream: who edits that array, and on what evidence? If it gets edited by hand because somebody tried four prompts and the output looked fine, the system is laundering vibes through a type system. At Dex , same architecture, real traffic, the equivalent of that array was edited by exactly one thing: the eval suite. A model earned a class by passing the class’s eval, and lost it the same way. No meeting could move a model up the catalog. A green run could. What a contract looks like An eval-as-contract has four parts, per prompt class: A fixed dataset. Real cases, frozen at a version. Not “we’ll try some prompts”: a file in the repo, diffable, reviewed like code. A pass criterion per case. Mechanical wherever possible. A threshold over the dataset. The bar, as a number. A consequence. The threshold gates the catalog. Fail the eval, lose the class. Two sketches, one mechanical and one judged. Extraction is the easy case, because correctness is checkable. The dataset is a few hundred input documents with hand-verified expected fields; the criterion is exact match on the JSON keys that matter: // evals/extraction.eval.ts export default { class: 'extractive' , dataset: 'datasets/extraction-v7.jsonl' , // 240 frozen cases grade : ( got , want ) => [ 'order_id' , 'total' , 'currency' ]. every (( k ) => deepEqual (got[k], want[k])), threshold: 0.98 , // below this, the model loses the class }; No judge model, no partial credit. Either total is 128.40 or it isn’t. When a candidate small model scores 0.99 on this, “good enough for extraction” stops being an opinion. Reasoning needs a criterion that fits the task. Code can be checked by running it; some answers can be compared with known results. When those checks are insufficient, a stronger model can grade a rubric: did the answer identify the actual root cause, did it propose a fix that compiles against the stated constraints, did it avoid inventing APIs. Three binary checks per case, a case passes at 3/3, and the threshold sits over the case pass rate. Rubric grading is noisier than exact match, so the dataset is bigger and the rubric itself is versioned; when the rubric changes, every model regrades, and the diff shows exactly which cases flipped. The output of a run is one number per model per class. The catalog is whatever those numbers say it is. Two common pitfalls A bar can fail in exactly two directions, and they are not symmetric in how they hurt. Too low , and silent quality regressions ship. The routing layer happily sends structured-output traffic to the smallest model, the eval stays green because the dataset never covered nested objects, and three weeks later support tickets are your eval suite. This failure is invisible at the routing layer: every metric the system emits (latency, cost, error rate) improves while the product quietly gets worse. The only instrument that can catch it is the eval, which is precisely the instrument that’s broken. Too high , and you never realise the savings. A 0.999 bar on extraction, scored against a dataset full of adversarial edge cases that are roughly nonexistent in production, keeps everything pinned to the expensive tier. Nobody files a ticket about money you didn’t save. On our traffic mix at Dex, the bulk of requests were cheap-class; an over-tight bar on just those classes would have erased most of the win described in the cost study . Too low is a correctness bug. Too high is a silent cost bug. You tune between them the same way you tune anything: by looking at what the eval missed and what it over-weighted, against production reality. Evals rot Which brings up the uncomfortable part: production reality moves. An eval dataset is a snapshot of a traffic distribution, and traffic distributions shift. Users find new phrasings. The product grows a feature that produces a prompt shape the dataset has never seen. The classifier starts binning things into a class whose dataset predates the pattern. None of this turns the suite red; it turns it stale , which is worse, because stale looks identical to green. Treat eval datasets like dependency updates. On a cadence (for us, roughly monthly, plus whenever a new prompt pattern landed) sample recent production traffic per class, label it, fold it into the dataset, bump the version, re-run every model. Sometimes a model loses a class it had held for months. That’s not the process failing; that’s the process working. A recorded demo needs the same discipline. If the implementation changes, old examples need to be checked again rather than presented as evidence of the new behavior. A frozen dataset is honest about the past. Only a refreshed one is honest about the present. Contracts are cultural The deepest effect was never technical. An eval suite is the API contract between the routing layer and the product : the routing layer promises “anything I send to a model, that model has cleared”, and the product team gets to define what clearing means, in cases, in a file, under review. That changes the shape of disagreements. “Is the small model good enough for extraction?” used to be a meeting: someone pastes two outputs into a channel, someone else counters with a cherry-picked failure, and whoever cares more wins. With the contract in place, the same disagreement is a pull request: here are thirty cases where the small model fails, add them to the dataset, run the suite, read the number. If the number drops below threshold, the model loses the class and the system stops sending it that traffic, automatically. If it doesn’t, the thirty cases stay in the dataset as a permanent regression guard, and the savings stay on. Diffs against a dataset, instead of vibes against a screenshot. That is what makes the routing promise honest. The cheapest model that clears the bar is a great architecture and a meaningless sentence, until the bar is written down, runnable, versioned, and allowed to say no.

blog/graph-traversal-typescript-python/i.description: Choose BFS, DFS, or Dijkstra from the question and edge weights. Adjacency-list examples in Python and TypeScript, with the assumptions each algorithm needs.
blog/graph-traversal-typescript-python/i.title: BFS, DFS, and Dijkstra in TypeScript and Python · Tomas Brasca
blog/graph-traversal-typescript-python/i.prose: In the data structures field guide , graphs got a row in the table and a promise of their own post. This is that post, and it starts with the thing that makes graphs different from every other row: you almost never instantiate one. There is no Graph class to memorize. A graph is a hash map from node to neighbor list, built in four lines, and everything interesting lives in how you walk it. from collections import defaultdict graph: dict[ int , list[ int ]] = defaultdict( list ) for u, v in edges: graph[u].append(v) graph[v].append(u) # undirected, drop this line for directed const graph = new Map < number , number []>(); for ( const [ u , v ] of edges) { if ( ! graph. has (u)) graph. set (u, []); if ( ! graph. has (v)) graph. set (v, []); graph. get (u) ! . push (v); graph. get (v) ! . push (u); // undirected } That is the adjacency list, and it is the right representation for nearly everything: O(V + E) space, O(1) edge insertion, neighbors iterable in degree time. The adjacency matrix earns its O(V²) memory only when the graph is dense or you need O(1) “is there an edge between u and v?” queries. From there, two booleans select the algorithm: Question Unweighted Weighted Shortest path BFS Dijkstra if weights ≥ 0 Reachability / components BFS or DFS BFS or DFS Cycle detection, topological order DFS DFS Negative edge weights n/a Bellman-Ford (rare) The three implementations below cover reachability and shortest paths with equal or nonnegative edge weights. They differ mainly in how they manage the frontier. DFS structure questions also need entry and exit state. BFS: the queue visits in distance order BFS’s bet: process nodes in the order they were discovered, and you process them in order of distance from the start. The invariant is worth saying out loud ( the queue only ever holds nodes at distance d and d+1, in that order ) because it is the entire proof that the first time you reach a node is the shortest way to reach it. That only holds when every edge costs the same, which is why BFS is the unweighted column of the table. from collections import deque def bfs (graph: dict[ int , list[ int ]], start: int ) -> dict[ int , int ]: dist = {start: 0 } queue = deque([start]) while queue: node = queue.popleft() for neighbor in graph.get(node, []): if neighbor not in dist: dist[neighbor] = dist[node] + 1 queue.append(neighbor) return dist The queue trap from the field guide shows up here on schedule: Python’s deque.popleft() is O(1), but the literal TypeScript translation uses Array.shift() and goes quietly quadratic on large graphs. The dependency-free fix is a read-index: never remove anything, just walk a pointer forward: function bfs ( graph : Map < number , number []>, start : number ) : Map < number , number > { const dist = new Map ([[start, 0 ]]); const queue = [start]; let head = 0 ; // read-index: O(1) "dequeue", no shift() while (head < queue. length ) { const node = queue[head ++ ]; for ( const neighbor of graph. get (node) ?? []) { if ( ! dist. has (neighbor)) { dist. set (neighbor, dist. get (node) ! + 1 ); queue. push (neighbor); } } } return dist; } One detail that separates working BFS from subtly-broken BFS: mark nodes visited when you enqueue them , not when you dequeue them. Mark-on-dequeue lets the same node enter the queue many times through different neighbors, and on a dense graph that turns O(V + E) into something much worse, without changing the answers, which is exactly the kind of bug a contest judge punishes with “time limit exceeded” and production punishes with a pager. DFS: the stack answers structure questions Swap the queue for a stack and you get DFS. The distance-order guarantee is gone; what you get instead is completion order in a full DFS implementation, where a node finishes after its DFS descendants, and that is the property behind every structural question: does this graph have a cycle? What order do these dependencies resolve in? How many islands are there? The recursive version uses the call stack. This minimal example records reachability; a structural traversal also needs entry and exit bookkeeping: def dfs (graph: dict[ int , list[ int ]], node: int , visited: set[ int ]) -> None : visited.add(node) for neighbor in graph.get(node, []): if neighbor not in visited: dfs(graph, neighbor, visited) And here is the production gotcha neither language warns you about: recursion depth is an input-dependent resource. Python has a configurable recursion limit, commonly around 1,000 frames in CPython; a path graph with 10,000 nodes crashes correct code with RecursionError . JavaScript also has an engine-dependent call-stack limit and can throw a RangeError . Neither limit is an algorithmic guarantee. sys.setrecursionlimit is a band-aid; the real fix is the iterative version with an explicit stack, which is the same algorithm with the resource limit moved from the runtime to the heap: function dfs ( graph : Map < number , number []>, start : number ) : Set < number > { const visited = new Set ([start]); const stack = [start]; while (stack. length ) { const node = stack. pop () ! ; for ( const neighbor of graph. get (node) ?? []) { if ( ! visited. has (neighbor)) { visited. add (neighbor); stack. push (neighbor); } } } return visited; } For an undirected graph, running a reachability traversal from each unvisited node counts connected components. The iterative example above does not record DFS completion order. Topological sorting needs explicit exit frames or a separate algorithm such as Kahn’s. For a directed graph, encountering a node currently on the DFS recursion path signals a cycle. In an undirected graph, also distinguish the parent edge from a back edge. On a directed acyclic graph, reversing DFS finishing order gives a topological order. All the structure questions are DFS plus one extra piece of bookkeeping. Dijkstra: BFS where the queue becomes a heap Give edges unequal nonnegative weights and BFS’s shortest-path guarantee breaks: the first time you reach a node is no longer the cheapest. The repair is to always expand the cheapest known frontier node instead of the oldest, which means the queue becomes a min-heap, which means this is the heap gap from the field guide all over again: Python has heapq , TypeScript has nothing. import heapq def dijkstra (graph: dict[ int , list[tuple[ int , int ]]], start: int ) -> dict[ int , int ]: dist = {start: 0 } heap = [( 0 , start)] # (cost, node) while heap: cost, node = heapq.heappop(heap) if cost > dist.get(node, float ( "inf" )): continue # stale entry, skip for neighbor, weight in graph.get(node, []): new_cost = cost + weight if new_cost < dist.get(neighbor, float ( "inf" )): dist[neighbor] = new_cost heapq.heappush(heap, (new_cost, neighbor)) return dist The subtle line is the stale-entry skip. heapq has no decrease-key operation, so when a cheaper route to a node is found, the old, more expensive heap entry is not removed; it is left to rot and discarded when it surfaces. That “lazy deletion” is the standard trick, it keeps the complexity at O((V + E) log V), and forgetting the skip gives you an algorithm that is correct but re-expands nodes for no reason. In TypeScript, you face the same choice as in the field guide: for interview-sized inputs, a sorted array wearing a heap’s interface is fine if you say the cost out loud ; for production, a priority-queue dependency is one of the few data-structure imports that genuinely earns its place in package.json . The recognition table You hear You reach for ”Fewest hops / moves / steps” BFS ”Can A reach B?” BFS or DFS, either ”Cheapest route”, weights ≥ 0 Dijkstra ”Valid build/course order” DFS topological sort ”How many groups/islands?” DFS components (or Union-Find) “Is there a circular dependency?” DFS with on-path tracking The deeper habit is noticing that a graph problem rarely announces itself as one. Package dependencies, currency conversion chains, social follows, state machines, spreadsheet cell references: none of these say “graph” in the ticket. The skill the contest table drills is hearing nodes and edges in a problem that was stated in nouns and verbs, and then asking the only two questions that matter: are the edges weighted, and what do I actually need: a distance, an order, or a yes/no. Two booleans and a question. The algorithm picks itself.

blog/how-to-get-a-job-in-big-2026/index..description: What I practiced, where I applied, and what I learned from a remote job search, including the system design rounds I did not pass.
blog/how-to-get-a-job-in-big-2026/index..title: Notes from a software engineering job search · Tomas Brasca
blog/how-to-get-a-job-in-big-2026/index..prose: When I started looking for a remote engineering role, I needed to decide what to practice, where to apply, and how to explain the work I had already done. These are notes from that search, not a universal hiring roadmap. This started as a conversation with a friend about how we could both land a remote job, and it turned into the roadmap I wish someone had handed me. It organizes my own path, and maybe you leave with a tool you hadn’t heard of, or with confirmation for one you had. Where I’m speaking from I started searching two months ago. Right now I have four offers, most of them from consultancies. I also got deep into two product companies but didn’t pass their last technical round, mainly because system design is my weak spot, and that round usually sits right before the behavioural. I have five years of full-stack experience. I did competitive programming, so algorithms are the comfortable part: I can analyze and present a solution for pretty much any LeetCode medium. Hards are another story. They combine several patterns under tight constraints, sometimes with an advanced structure on top, and while big tech runs mostly on mediums too, the hards show up in their onsites and senior loops. I decided that grind wasn’t for me this round. Two things are non-negotiable wherever you apply. English, and understanding the business: in every interview you should know what they’re building and ask good questions about it. The third thing changed since my last job hunt: being a builder matters now. They want to see design principles, that you can work with AI, and that you communicate well. You need to sell what you build, and sell yourself as the person who built it. The AI part is big enough that it gets its own section below. Before any meeting Polish your LinkedIn first. There’s plenty of advice out there; what worked for me: A generic but clean cover image. A profile photo that looks professional. A shorter headline with strong words. A portfolio. Mine is simple on purpose, but a good one can also show your design taste. Experience and personal projects actually up to date. Your résumé Tools first. resume.io if you want a clean result fast and don’t care about the format underneath. If you do care, build it in Typst instead: the silver-dev-cv package gives you a résumé that typesets like LaTeX, plain text you can diff and version, without LaTeX’s own learning curve. And Silver.dev’s behavioural checker is worth a pass on your HR-screen answers too, not just the résumé. Mine is a plain-text Typst file: resume.typ , compiled with typst compile resume.typ cv.pdf . Take it as a starting point, not a template to copy verbatim, since the whole point above is editing it per company. The rules I actually follow once the document exists: Match your LinkedIn, don’t mirror it. They will open both tabs side by side. Any discrepancy between the two plants a doubt, and doubt tends to turn into rejection. Same story, not the same sentence twice. Edit the résumé per company. Find people who already work there on LinkedIn; their profiles provide clues about the team’s work, not proof of why any individual was hired. Borrow their title phrasing, reorder your bullets toward what their listing asks for, and pick the two or three experiences that tell the story that fits this specific role, not the complete story of your career. Write a per-company “about.” It should answer, explicitly or between the lines, “why should this company hire me” for this exact role. A generic summary answers no one’s question. No photo, no cover image. Common in Argentina, close to taboo at US companies. Cut it for anything outside the local market. Proofread every edit. A grammar checker can help, but read the final PDF yourself for errors, broken links, and awkward phrasing. No stars, bars, or 1-to-5 scores next to your skills. They read as invented precision. List the skill, prove the level in the experience bullets instead. Don’t link a GitHub with nothing on it. An empty-looking profile invites a question you don’t want asked in the room. Link it once it has real projects or contributions, not before. Where I actually apply LinkedIn is the default and I still use it, but these are the boards that earned more per hour I spent on them: Wellfound for startup roles. Listings publish salary and equity ranges up front, which kills the processes that were never going to match before they eat three of your evenings. Work at a Startup , the YC board. Fewer rounds and a faster answer, but each round is more intense, and you’re usually talking to a founder instead of a recruiter. Hacker News’ monthly “Who is hiring?” thread. No platform, no recruiter in the middle: you email or reply straight into the listing. Slower per application, but the reply rate is the highest of anything on this list. Himalayas and We Work Remotely when I want the search pre-filtered to remote-first companies instead of filtering LinkedIn’s noise myself. Built In if you’re open to hybrid and want a sense of which city’s scene is hiring, salary bands included there too. Applying is the cheap part of all this. Every one of these rewards a portfolio link that works far more than a cover letter that says nothing. The stages Almost every process I went through looked like this: 01 HR screen behavioural, act I 02 Technical interview async or sync 03 System design often folded into 04 outside big tech 04 Manager / founder / CEO behavioural, encore 05 Client interview staff-aug bonus level The pipeline. Dashed = the consultancy bonus level. Two footnotes from the trenches. Outside big tech, step 3 is often not a formal system design round: at consultancies and small product companies it becomes a technical-depth conversation, or gets merged into the final meeting. And if the consultancy does staff augmentation, expect a bonus round where the client interviews you again after you already passed everything. The behavioural questions rarely get their own stage; they’re sprinkled into the HR screen and the final meeting. The HR screen My notes call this stage RRHH, because Spanish. Your recruiter calls it HR. Here you need to convince a person that you’re a good match for the role. Explain things simply. Communication is everything. What works for me is preparing answers before the questions arrive. They usually follow from the role, so ask an AI what’s likely to come up and do your own research on top. Then there are the evergreens: the last thing you built and how, your current AI workflow, the most challenging thing you’ve done, your biggest mistake in production, the next thing you want to learn. I keep a tested file of answers that I know sound like me. Think of it as the script for a play where you’re a famous enough actor to improvise: you can change the lines, but you’d better know the play. answers.md tested answers improvise here The script: answers you have tested out loud, and the line you are allowed to improvise. My rules for this stage: Don’t blame others in your answers. Own what you did. When a story involves asking a more experienced teammate for help, say so. You can’t know everything, and solo players have a bad reputation. Your AI workflow can’t be “I ask Claude and turn on plan mode.” Research real ways of working with AI. More on this below. The technical interview Usually the second step. Sometimes it’s the first. Whatever, you prepare the same way. My advice: practice one language until it’s boring, and if they propose another, ask whether you can use yours. There’s too much to learn in 2026 to maintain two interview languages, and most companies let you pick any mainstream one anyway. The exceptions are domain rounds: a front-end interview will be JavaScript, a mobile one speaks whatever the platform speaks, and consultancy tests are sometimes tied to the client’s stack. For practice I recommend LeetCode or any platform like it, though I prefer NeetCode : the curated lists (the NeetCode 150 is free) give you structure instead of a pile of thousands of unsorted problems. I run one of those study plans as fast as I can, and in the process I only use AI to ask how a solution could be more performant or which more advanced concept applies. Not to solve the problem for me. The data structures you should be able to build and use: Arrays -> static and dynamic, and how they differ under the hood. Queue and stack -> the classic Valid Parentheses problem teaches a pattern you’ll reuse everywhere. Linked lists -> easy to understand, and reversing one is the canonical warm-up: before head 1 2 3 null after head null 1 2 3 every next pointer, flipped Walk it once, flip every next pointer, the tail becomes the new head. Hash tables -> must know. No negotiation on this one. Binary trees -> good to know, and the exercises are genuinely fun. B-trees -> good to know conceptually. Nearly every mainstream database (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, MongoDB) uses the B-tree family (usually B+ trees) for its indexes, and often for the table data itself. Nobody will ask you to implement one; they’ll ask why an index makes a query fast, and when it doesn’t help. Tries -> autocomplete. Elasticsearch’s completion suggester runs on trie-shaped automata, so this one is not just interview folklore. Probabilistic structures -> Bloom filters (RocksDB and Cassandra use them to skip files that can’t contain your key), HyperLogLog, count-min sketch. Honesty: outside big tech these live in system design conversations, not coding rounds. And at minimum these algorithms: Recursion. DFS and BFS. Binary search, and not just the code: understand why it works. The three resources I actually work through, in the order I reach for them: The NeetCode roadmap when I want to study by pattern and see which topic depends on which. LeetCode 75 when a process starts next week and I want the shortest path back to sharp. Frontend Masters’ algorithms course if you have time and would rather be taught than grind. It’s behind a paid subscription, and it’s the one that rebuilds intuition rather than speed. I’ve written a longer field guide to these structures and a whole post on binary search beyond arrays if you want to go deeper. The take-home Sometimes stage 2 isn’t a call, it’s a repo. This one sucks if you already have a job, because it spends a weekend you didn’t budget. I do mine on a Saturday and I cap it at four or five hours. Be honest about the time. They read commit timestamps, so “I gave it one afternoon, here’s what I’d do with another day” is a fine answer and a suspiciously polished twenty-hour submission is not, even when it’s better. 0h 1h 2h 3h 4h 5h scope build README ship hard stop One Saturday. The cap is the point — everything that scores fits inside it. What I optimize for, in order: Get to the point. Find the actual need behind the prompt and why it exists. There’s a real problem underneath, and they’re hiring the person who can spot it, not the one who implements the spec literally. A clean UI/UX. Now that AI writes the boilerplate, a rough interface no longer reads as “I focused on the backend.” It reads as not caring. README and a clean architecture. Non-negotiable. The README is where you write down the trade-offs you took and what you’d do with another week, and it’s the document the review call runs on. Deploy it if you can. A URL beats a clone-and-run every time. The cap is doing as much work as the list. Scoping is the skill being tested, and a submission that clearly ate the whole weekend answers that question the wrong way. System design and CEO talks Honesty first: this is the round that knocked me out of two product companies, so read this section as notes from the guy who failed it, not the guy who passed it. One clarification so you don’t repeat my typo: the round is called system design. Architecture, APIs, database choices, scaling, trade-offs. A design system is a different thing entirely, the frontend artifact with component libraries and design tokens, and some frontend loops test that separately. What I can recommend: research the team you’d be joining and what they’re building, so the conversation can go toward the systems they actually run instead of a generic URL shortener. For learning the material itself, I recommend Matt Pocock’s /teach skill ( npx skills add mattpocock/skills --skill=teach ). It turns a directory into a study workspace your coding agent teaches from, pulling cited sources instead of answering from model memory. The final meeting with the manager or CEO doubles as the behavioural round, so your HR-screen script gets a second performance. The AI workflow question An interview may ask you to explain or demonstrate how you use AI. Prepare a concrete example of what you accepted, what you rejected, and how you checked the result. Ask the recruiter which tools are allowed in that specific round; policies vary by company and can change. What they evaluate is not the size of your rig. It’s judgment: when you rejected AI output, how you knew it was wrong, how you validate what your agents produce. “I ask Claude and turn on plan mode” dies at the first follow-up question. A practiced setup, rules files, agents, a repeatable workflow you can rebuild in front of someone, helps you demo that judgment convincingly. But the setup is the prop; the review habits are the act. your prompt the agent its output your review reject, refine, again ship The loop they actually grade. The rig is scenery; the amber box is the act. The workflow I describe when they ask is iterative and vertical. Generate, test, generate again, with each pass shipping a thin but complete slice of the product instead of a horizontal layer of it. And write the decisions down as you go: a short product doc per slice recording why A and not B. Those docs are the whole difference between “the agent wrote it” and “I directed it,” and they’re what you read from when someone asks you why. Which makes the cheapest preparation obvious. Whatever you build as a showcase, build it with the workflow you plan to describe. The project becomes the portfolio link, and the process becomes the answers. Get explicit permission before using AI in an assessment. Your normal development workflow does not determine the rules of an interview. The open questions Things I’m still researching, and I owe each of them its own post: How is AI changing the process from the company’s side? Startups vs mid-size companies. Is LeetCode dead? (I just told you to grind it, so: not yet.) System design book recommendations. What does the survivor profile look like? If you have answers to any of these, my inbox is open. Meanwhile I’ll be in some HR screen, improvising from my script.
