blog/rate-limiting-inference/index.html.description: What per-IP limits, a shared counter, and request caps can control, and why a KV-backed quota is not a strict spending guarantee.
blog/rate-limiting-inference/index.html.title: Rate-limiting a public inference endpoint · Tomas Brasca
blog/rate-limiting-inference/index.html.prose: The portfolio agent accepts questions from anonymous visitors and makes model calls billed to my account. Before exposing that endpoint, I need to decide what stops a script from turning the demo into an ongoing expense. A request limit helps, but a request limit and a spending guarantee are different contracts. This article describes the controls in the current implementation, including where their guarantees stop. Updated October 2026. The original router demo has been replaced by an A2UI agent. The old article’s five-per-minute limit and per-request cost examples no longer described the endpoint. The current controls are documented below. Start with the request path The browser sends a question to /api/a2ui . The endpoint checks that the agent is configured, validates the question, consumes the rate-limit budgets, and only then calls the model. The request boundary accepts a message of at most 400 characters and trims client-supplied history. The agent includes its own instructions and retrieved portfolio context as well, so 400 characters is not a bound on the full input token count. The agent defaults to anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5 , allows a model override through configuration, and requests at most 2,048 output tokens. Those settings constrain a call. They do not establish a permanent dollar ceiling independent of model choice, input context, or provider pricing. Three windows, checked in order The controls in src/lib/ratelimit.ts are: Window Configured allowance Purpose Per IP, per minute 3 turns Slow repeated submissions. Per IP, per UTC day 5 turns Give each visitor a small allowance. Shared, per UTC day 300 turns Target an aggregate daily request budget. These are configured allowances, not exact distributed admission guarantees. The endpoint checks burst, visitor, and shared budgets in that order. A request rejected by the first check does not consume the later ones. The per-IP controls return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. If the shared counter reports exhaustion, the endpoint returns HTTP 503 with a retry time. That distinction lets the interface explain whether a visitor’s allowance or the site’s shared allowance is exhausted. The counter has two parts Each bucket uses a fixed window based on Unix time. The bucket and window identify the KV key. When the window changes, new requests use a different key; old entries expire through KV’s TTL. An in-memory counter increments before the first asynchronous operation. That prevents two requests in the same isolate from both reading the same local count before either consumes it. KV then provides persistence across requests that reach other isolates. The local counter is useful, but it does not coordinate all of Cloudflare’s isolates. It is also cleared when an isolate restarts. Its correctness boundary is one running isolate, not the entire deployment. A turn consumes its allowance before the upstream call. Failed upstream calls are therefore still attempts against the allowance. That is conservative for abuse control, although it means a failed answer can cost the visitor a question. Where KV stops being a quota Workers KV is eventually consistent. Separate locations can read stale counts, and concurrent writes can overwrite one another. Cloudflare also documents a limit of one write per second to the same key. A shared daily key can encounter that write limit even when the inference service itself has capacity. See Cloudflare’s KV write guidance . Those properties prevent this implementation from promising exactly 300 admitted turns across the whole deployment. The in-memory counter narrows one race; it does not make distributed read-modify-write atomic. There is no measured, fixed multiplier that justifies saying over-admission is always small. When the requirement is an exact shared quota, use a coordination mechanism that supports the needed atomic decision. Cloudflare recommends Durable Objects when stronger consistency is required . That would be a different implementation, not a property this counter already has. Missing storage is a distinct failure mode If the KV binding is absent, the current limiter continues with its in-isolate counter. That supports local development, but in production it would remove durable coordination and allow fresh allowances as isolates restart or multiply. A low per-call cost does not make unlimited aggregate traffic bounded. The production choice needs to be explicit: refuse live requests when the required storage is missing, or accept that the limiter is best-effort and enforce a separate spending boundary. The article can state that tradeoff honestly without pretending the stricter policy is already implemented. Bound the bill separately A cost estimate starts with admitted calls, input and output tokens, model prices, and any additional attempts. Every term needs a stated assumption. Multiplying a soft request limit by a cheap call does not turn either into a hard global cap. For a public demo, I want both useful application controls and an independent provider-side spending limit where one is available. I also want a clear way to disable live inference. These are requirements for a stronger budget contract, not claims about controls that this repository has already proven. The Flagship case study explains the interface and agent architecture. The lesson here is narrower: describe a limiter by the coordination it actually provides. Call a target a target, and reserve “guarantee” for a bound the implementation can enforce.

blog/routing-beats-scaling/index.html.description: A worked example of inference routing, its classification overhead, and the eval bar that makes a cheaper model a defensible choice.
blog/routing-beats-scaling/index.html.title: Routing before scaling: the cost arithmetic · Tomas Brasca
blog/routing-beats-scaling/index.html.prose: When an LLM feature gets too expensive, the instinct is to treat it as an infrastructure problem. Cache aggressively. Trim the prompt. Batch where you can. Negotiate committed-use pricing. All of these are real, and on a good day they compound into a respectable saving, call it tens of percent. None of them touches the dominant term: which model you call . Model prices can differ substantially. Whether routing saves money depends on that spread, the traffic mix, classification overhead, retries, and the quality each model can maintain. A large price difference creates an opportunity, not a guarantee. At Dex I got to test this on production traffic. This post is the argument and the arithmetic, with the parts I’m allowed to share. The default instinct The feature started where most LLM features start: one model, the biggest available tier, on every request. That is a reasonable place to start: quality is whatever the best model gives you, and there is exactly one integration to maintain. It is an unreasonable place to stay. The bill scales linearly with usage, so the better the feature does, the worse it looks in the cost review. And the traffic that drives the volume is rarely the traffic that needs the horsepower. Pull a sample of real requests and read them. A large share are short and nearly mechanical: pull a field out of a message, summarise a paragraph, reformat a list. Sending those to a frontier model is paying for reasoning capacity the request cannot use. Classify, then dispatch The router does two things, in that order. Classify. Every prompt gets bucketed into one of four classes: extractive , structured , reasoning , creative . The classes are defined by what failure looks like, not by topic. An extractive request fails by missing the field; a structured one fails by emitting malformed output; a reasoning one fails by being wrong in the middle of a chain; a creative one fails by being dull. Different failure modes need different amounts of model. An earlier version of this portfolio demonstrated the idea with a heuristic classifier. This example is historical; the current playground is an A2UI portfolio agent: /** Heuristic classifier: cheap and instant; swap for a model call if needed. */ export function classify ( prompt : string ) : PromptClass { const p = prompt. toLowerCase (); if ( / \b json \b|\b extract \b|\b parse \b|\b schema \b| as json | key [- ] ? value |\b csv \b|\b table \b / . test (p)) { return 'structured' ; } if ( / stack trace | debug | root cause |\b fix \b|\b why \b| explain | reason | prove | step [- ] by [- ] step | complexity | algorithm / . test ( p, ) ) { return 'reasoning' ; } if ( / haiku | poem | story | rhyme | write a | tagline | slogan | creative | lyric / . test (p)) { return 'creative' ; } return prompt. length > 280 ? 'reasoning' : 'extractive' ; } In production at Dex the classifier was itself a small, cheap model call with a strict label set, because real traffic is messier than regexes. The contract is identical either way: cheap classification first, and when in doubt, escalate; note the fallthrough sends long ambiguous prompts to reasoning , not to extractive . Misrouting up costs money; misrouting down costs quality. Dispatch. The catalog is a list of models ordered cheapest to dearest, where each entry declares which classes it clears . Dispatch is then a single walk: function pickModel ( cls : PromptClass , env : Record < string , string | undefined >) : CatalogEntry | null { for ( const entry of CATALOG ) { if (entry.clears. includes (cls) && env[entry.keyName]) return entry; } return null ; } That is the entire decision. The first model that both clears the class and has a configured key wins. In that historical demo catalog, llama-3.1-8b-instant on Groq ($0.05/M input tokens) clears extractive and creative ; gpt-4o-mini ($0.15/M) adds structured ; qwen-2.5-72b ($0.35/M) is the only entry that clears reasoning . Even within this deliberately cheap public catalog the spread is 7x. Add a frontier tier at the top, as a production catalog does, and the spread depends on the models and prices at the time. These figures describe the old demo, not current provider pricing. Cost is computed from real token usage, not estimated: const usd = (reply.promptTokens * entry.inPrice + reply.completionTokens * entry.outPrice) / 1_000_000 ; An illustrative request The following rates are assumptions for the arithmetic, not a current price quote or a measured production benchmark. Production outcomes below are qualitative accounts of employer work. Run the arithmetic on a typical extractive request, say 300 prompt tokens and a 150-token completion. On llama-3.1-8b-instant at $0.05/$0.08 per million tokens, that call costs $0.000027 . The same call on a hypothetical frontier model priced at $2.50/$10 per million costs about $0.00225. That is an 80x difference for a request, provided the smaller model passes the same acceptance criteria. Include the classifier call, fallbacks, and repeated attempts before treating this as end-to-end savings. On the Dex traffic mix, the large majority of requests classified as extractive or short-form structured. Once those classes moved to small models, cost per request on them dropped by roughly an order of magnitude, and because they dominated the volume, total inference spend fell by most of its previous value. The expensive tier was still there; it just stopped being the default and became the escalation path for the minority of requests that actually needed it. The part nobody predicted in the planning doc: tail latency tightened too . Small models are fast, and small models on fast inference hardware are very fast. The old p95 was dominated by the big model’s long generations on trivial requests; after routing, the trivial requests came back in a few hundred milliseconds and the p95 reflected only the work that deserved to be slow. Routing is usually pitched as a cost lever. On our mix it was a latency lever that happened to pay for itself. The catch Routing changes the quality decision from “always use the best model” to “use the cheapest model that passes”. That sentence does no work unless passes means something. Each clears entry in the catalog is supposed to be a cached verdict from an eval suite: this model, on this class of request, meets the bar we defined before we cared about the bill. Set the bar too low and the system ships quality regressions invisibly, one cheap dispatch at a time. Set it too high and you never realise the savings, because everything escalates. Either way the catalog is lying to the dispatch loop. This is why evals are contracts , not dashboards. At Dex the implementation itself was a small amount of code: classify, walk, dispatch, fall back. The engineering time went into writing honest per-class evals and keeping them green as models and prompts changed underneath. The routing decision is exactly as trustworthy as the test that gates it, and no more. Where to inspect the design The Dex case study describes the routing architecture and its tradeoffs. Evals are contracts explains what must justify the catalog’s quality claims. The current playground demonstrates a different system. It answers questions about this portfolio with interfaces built through A2UI. It does not let you compare model routes. The Flagship case study documents that implementation.

blog/static-site-dynamic-demo/index.html.description: A historical build log of the router demo: prerendered pages, one interactive island, and one server endpoint. The demo changed; the boundary still matters.
blog/static-site-dynamic-demo/index.html.title: Why a static site shows a dynamic demo · Tomas Brasca
blog/static-site-dynamic-demo/index.html.prose: This post describes the original router demo. In July 2026, an A2UI portfolio agent replaced it. The examples and API path below are historical; the current endpoint is /api/a2ui . The original design combined prerendered pages with one interactive demo that ran inference on demand. The static half is easy to defend. The people this site is written for open dev tools out of habit. If a page that claims I build production systems takes three seconds to hydrate a hero animation, the claim is dead before the first paragraph. So: prerendered HTML, real CSS, no framework runtime. Astro does this by default and does it well. The problem is the centerpiece. The contradiction The thing this site most needs to show is a live AI demo : a visitor types a prompt, the system classifies it, dispatches to the cheapest model that clears the bar across OpenAI, Groq and OpenRouter, and shows latency, cost and output side by side. That is real inference. Real inference is about as far from static as a web page gets: it needs client state, a network call, server-side API keys, and a rate limiter so the public internet cannot run up my bill. A static site whose hook is dynamic. The whole build is the resolution of that contradiction. The split The resolution: everything is prerendered except exactly two things. One React island, mounted on the homepage: < Playground client:visible /> And one on-demand route, which runs as a Cloudflare Worker: // The ONE on-demand route. Everything else on the site is static. export const prerender = false ; That comment is in the actual source. Every page (homepage, case studies, every blog post including this one) is HTML generated at build time. The island is the only client-side state. The Worker route is the only server-side compute. The keys live in the Worker’s environment and never touch the client. When a visitor opts into live mode, the request path is short: ┌ Playground island (browser) │ POST /api/route { prompt } ▼ ┌ Cloudflare Worker │ 1. liveAvailable? → 503 if no keys │ 2. rate limit (KV) → 429, 5/min per IP │ 3. classify(prompt) → extractive | structured | reasoning | creative │ 4. cheapest model that clears the class ▼ ┌ Provider (Groq / OpenAI / OpenRouter) │ one chat completion, 512 tokens max ▼ └ RouteResult { model, latency, cost, why, response } → back to the island, rendered like any demo run Four hops, one of which is optional by design. Most visitors never trigger it. Demo by default The island does not boot into live mode. It boots into demo mode: four pre-recorded routes, bundled into the island itself as plain TypeScript. Here is one, verbatim from src/lib/router/fixtures.ts : { key : 'summarize' , prompt : 'Summarize this release note in three bullets.' , model : 'llama-3.1-8b' , provider : 'Groq' , tone : 'sage' , latency : '240 ms' , cost : '$0.00004' , why : 'Extractive and short, the smallest model clears the bar.' , response : '• Auth tokens now rotate every 24 hours. \n • Webhook retries are capped at 5 with backoff. \n • Node 16 is dropped; minimum runtime is Node 18.' , }, The fixtures are recordings of real runs, refreshed when the routing logic or providers change. Switching between them re-renders the full result (model, provider, latency, cost, routing rationale, response) with zero network. Free, instant, abuse-proof. The usual way to show off a system like this is a video or a GIF. Fixtures beat both, for three reasons. A GIF plays at its own pace; fixtures let the reader poke at the part they care about, in whatever order, for as long as they want. A video is dead weight: a 4 MB MP4 to show 2 KB of structured data. The four fixtures cost less than a single screenshot. And a recording proves nothing about the interface: with fixtures, the demo runs through the exact same React component, the same result rendering, the same state machine as a live route. The only thing demo mode fakes is the network call. Everything the reader sees is the real product surface. What islands actually buy here client:visible is doing more work than it looks like. Astro renders the Playground’s initial HTML at build time, so the section is visible and styled before any JavaScript arrives. The framework runtime and component code are only fetched when the island scrolls into the viewport: not on page load, not on idle, on visible . A reader who lands on a blog post and leaves gets effectively no JavaScript. A reader who opens the homepage but never scrolls to the Playground also gets none of the island’s code. Only the reader who arrives at the demo pays for the demo, and by then the static HTML has long since finished rendering, so the cost is invisible. Interactivity is opt-in per component, not a tax on every page. Measure the boundary The important accounting boundary is the route and component that require interaction. Check a production build and the browser’s network panel to see which assets load before the island becomes visible and which arrive afterward. The original bundle-size snapshot is not a useful description of today’s site. The agent, renderer, and cinematic pages have changed since then. A size claim needs its build revision, measurement method, and the assets it includes; the current Flagship case study is the place to follow the replacement architecture. The demo is the product The framing I kept coming back to while building this: the demo is the product; the live call is the flourish. The fixtures carry the argument: they show the routing decision, the cost spread, the latency spread, the rationale. Live mode exists so a sceptical reader can verify none of it is staged, which is why it gets real keys, a real rate limit , and a catalog of cheap models only. That ordering is what makes the contradiction dissolve. A static site cannot afford a dynamic centerpiece on every page load. It can absolutely afford one island that wakes up when you look at it, and one Worker that answers only when you explicitly opt in. The full write-up of the system itself (classifier, catalog, blast-radius cap) is in the Flagship case study . Update, July 2026: the router demo this post describes has since been replaced by an A2UI conversational portfolio . The island-plus-Worker split it argues for did not change — only what runs inside it did, which is the point.

blog/the-unglamorous-middle/index.html.description: Joining my first startup after years of backend work, learning LLM infrastructure on the job, and finding the work that turns a demo into a product.
blog/the-unglamorous-middle/index.html.title: The unglamorous middle · Tomas Brasca
blog/the-unglamorous-middle/index.html.prose: I’d spent three and a half years making backends that didn’t fall over. Then I joined a startup, and learned that not falling over was the easy part. Before Dex I worked at scale. A few million users, e-commerce traffic that spiked on payday weekends and never apologised. The problems there were large but they were never vague : you knew the shape of the load, you knew which path could never lie, and there was enough structure around you that a careful engineer could be careful. I spent those years getting good at one thing, making a system stay correct under pressure, and I quietly assumed that was most of the job. Dex was my first real startup, and the first thing it taught me is that the structure I’d been taking for granted was load-bearing. Chaos after structure A startup at speed is a different climate, not just a faster version of the same one. The roadmap was a guess that got re-rolled every couple of weeks. The thing that was urgent on Monday was sometimes irrelevant by Thursday, because a customer call or a cost spike had rewritten the priorities underneath us. I wore more hats in my first month than in the previous three years combined: backend, a bit of infra, a bit of product, a lot of “whoever notices it owns it.” That sounds like a complaint. It isn’t. It was the most I’d ever learned in a fixed stretch of time, precisely because nothing waited for me to feel ready. Learning on the clock I came in as a backend engineer. The feature I was handed was an LLM feature, and I had never put a model into production in my life. Three and a half years of experience, and a lot of it didn’t transfer cleanly. Row-level locks and idempotency keys tell you nothing about how to make a model call cheap, or how to know whether a smaller model is “good enough,” or what happens to your product when someone else’s API has a bad night. I had to learn a new domain quickly, in public, against real traffic, with the meter running, because the alternative was the feature not shipping. And the feature demoed beautifully. That was the trap. The middle is the product An AI demo can look convincing before the product is reliable. You type a prompt, the model answers, the room nods. The demo dazzled me too, at first, until the bill arrived and I understood that the part everyone had been admiring was the part we hadn’t built. The model was rented. The floor on demo quality was set by someone else’s last training run, not by anything our team had done. Everything that turned that demo into a product lived somewhere much less photogenic: routing, rate limits, evals, fallbacks, cost ceilings. The unglamorous middle. Nobody puts it in the deck. It turned out to be the job, and, eventually, the place I was most useful. The feature had started where most LLM features start: one model, the biggest tier, on every request: the “pull the date out of this email” requests and the “reason through this contract” requests alike. So the bill scaled linearly with usage, and the better the feature did, the worse it looked in the cost review. The fix wasn’t clever. It was a router that classified each prompt and walked a catalog ordered cheapest-to-dearest, taking the first model that cleared the bar: for ( const entry of CATALOG ) { if (entry.clears. includes (cls) && env[entry.keyName]) return entry; } A few lines. The work was never those lines; it was earning the word clears . A bar set too low ships quality regressions one cheap call at a time; a bar set too high means everything escalates and you never see the savings. So most of my real effort went into writing honest per-class evals and keeping them green while the models and prompts shifted underneath. The routing logic was an afternoon. The contracts that made it trustworthy were the quarter. The rest of the middle was the same texture. A cap before a launch: no anonymous caller should be able to spend an unbounded amount of someone else’s money. A fallback, so a provider’s bad night degraded the product instead of taking it down. None of it was novel. All of it was the difference between a thing that demos and a thing that survives week two. What the startup taught me that scale didn’t At my old job I learned to find the one path that must never lie, make it small, and let everything else be eventually consistent. That instinct still serves me. But the startup taught me two things scale never had to. The first is that you can pick up an entire unfamiliar domain faster than you’d believe when there’s no one else to hand it to and the feature ships either way. I learned faster by taking a bounded piece of work, asking for help, and checking the result than by waiting to feel qualified. The second is that the work users actually pay for is almost never the work that looks impressive in a demo. It’s the answer that’s still there at 2 a.m., the bill that surprises nobody, the quality that’s the same on Thursday as it was on Monday. That’s not the boring part around the product. For me, three and a half years in and finally in a room moving fast enough to prove it, it was the product.

blog/what-icpc-trains-you-to-see/index.h.description: What transferred from competitive programming to production work: stating invariants, checking assumptions, and estimating the worst case before writing code.
blog/what-icpc-trains-you-to-see/index.h.title: What ICPC trains you to see · Tomas Brasca
blog/what-icpc-trains-you-to-see/index.h.prose: I haven’t often needed a segment tree in production. That is the standard objection to competitive programming as job training, and it is correct as far as it goes. Nobody at work has ever asked me for a suffix automaton. The data structures were never the transferable part. What transferred is a reflex the contest format beats into you: state the invariant, bound the worst case, and only then write code. I competed through university and made the ICPC South America finals. Years later, that reflex is the most-used thing I took from it. What the format actually drills An ICPC contest is five hours, three people, one machine, around a dozen problems. Rejected submissions can add penalty time when a problem is eventually solved, subject to the contest rules. That makes failed attempts expensive, but it does not impose a fixed budget of one wrong answer per problem. That penalty structure changes how you work. You cannot debug your way to correctness; the judge gives you one bit of feedback per submission. Strong teams converge on the same loop: Read the constraints first. n ≤ 10^5 and n ≤ 10^18 are different problems wearing the same statement. State the invariant. One sentence that must hold at every step, said out loud to a teammate before anyone touches the keyboard. Bound the complexity. Estimate the work against the input size and time limit. Constants depend on the language, hardware, and operations; a universal operations-per-second budget is not a guarantee. Then type. Typing is the cheapest step and the last one. The teams that beat us were rarely faster typists. They simply made fewer mistakes. A worked example Classic problem: longest subarray with sum at most S, elements non-negative, n up to 10^7. The instinct is to start typing two pointers. The trained move is to write the invariant first: At the end of each iteration, [l, r] is a valid window (sum ≤ S) and l is the smallest left index that makes it valid. long long sum = 0 ; int l = 0 , best = 0 ; for ( int r = 0 ; r < n; r ++ ) { sum += a[r]; // extend right while (sum > S) sum -= a[l ++ ]; // restore the invariant best = max (best, r - l + 1 ); // window valid, l minimal } Three things fall out of that one sentence, all before the code exists. Correctness. best is a maximum over windows where l is minimal for each r , so no longer valid window was skipped. Legality. The while loop only restores the invariant because the elements are non-negative: shrinking the window can never increase the sum. Put a single negative number in the array and the invariant becomes unmaintainable, and sliding window is the wrong technique entirely. The invariant does not just prove the solution; it tells you when the tool is illegal. Complexity. l and r each move at most n times, so the loop is O(n). 10^7 clears the budget with room. None of this is exotic. The point is the ordering: invariant, bound, code. Once that is a reflex, it does not switch off when the contest ends. The same reflex, in production Window math. The live endpoint on this site runs real LLM calls behind a per-IP rate limit on Cloudflare KV; the full design is its own post. The core of it: const window = Math. floor (nowSec / windowSec); const key = `rl:${ ip }:${ window }` ; Invariant: a key counts requests in exactly one window, and the counter only grows within it. Worst cases, stated before the code was written: a client straddling a window boundary can burst roughly twice the limit, and KV has no atomic increment, so concurrent requests can over-admit. Those are limitations of a soft limiter, not a proven global cost bound. The current implementation has changed; the rate-limit article distinguishes best-effort counters from a strict budget. That is contest analysis verbatim: find the adversarial input, bound the damage, decide whether the bound is acceptable. A greedy with a one-line proof. A simplified model router keeps its catalog ordered by cost and picks like this. This illustrates the routing work at Dex; it is not the current A2UI portfolio agent: function pickModel ( cls : PromptClass , env : Record < string , string | undefined >) : CatalogEntry | null { for ( const entry of CATALOG ) { if (entry.clears. includes (cls) && env[entry.keyName]) return entry; } return null ; } Cheapest-first is a greedy, and a greedy is only trustworthy when you can prove its property. Here the proof is one sentence: the catalog is sorted by price, so the first model that clears the class is the cheapest model that clears it . The production system I worked on at Dex runs the same shape across OpenAI, Groq and OpenRouter, and the cost case for it is the subject of routing beats scaling . Being able to state the greedy’s property in one line is what made the design easy to defend in review. Capacity planning as complexity analysis. The worst-case bill for a public inference endpoint is requests per window, times windows, times max tokens per request, times the dearest price in the catalog. A token limit can bound an individual call under stated assumptions. Bounding aggregate spend also requires a request cap that cannot be bypassed or over-admitted. The same habit applies when estimating a loop against a time limit: name the worst case before you ship, not after the invoice. What contests do not teach Honesty requires the other column. Contest code is write-only : it lives five hours, is read by nobody, and is full of variables named a , cnt and dp . Production code is read-mostly, and the contest teaches you nothing about that. It does not teach naming. It does not teach boring code; cleverness scores points in a contest and costs money in a codebase. It does not teach deletion; no judge has ever rewarded removing a feature. And it does not teach the timescale that matters at work: code that has to survive other people, changing requirements and your own forgetting, for years. I had to unlearn the compression instinct deliberately. Terse is fast under a clock. Terse is a liability in a repo. What transfers is everything that happens before the code, not the code. Coda: the boring strategy I also won the GTS algo-trading competition, and the win followed the same drill. Most entries optimised the average: maximum expected return per round. Mine was the boring one. I spent most of my time bounding the worst case (sizing positions so that no single bad sequence could knock the strategy out) and accepted a visibly lower mean to get that guarantee. The flashier strategies had better averages, right up until the tail showed up. Mine was still standing at the end, which is the only metric the scoreboard counted. That is the whole lesson in one contest. State what must stay true. Bound the worst case. Let the average take care of itself.
